senses.def: a container, primarily for liquids or wet objects
senses.comment: The vessels referred to in this context would no doubt have been rather large, containing perhaps some sixteen to twenty liters (or about four to five gallons).

senses.def: (derivative of Ἀδραμύττιον ‘Adramyttium,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to Adramyttium, a seaport in Mysia
to cause someone to become a prisoner of war
(a figurative extension of meaning of αἰχμαλωτίζω[a] ‘to take captive in war,’ 55.24) to gain complete control over, either by force or deception
one whose occupation is to catch fish
to assist by intervening on behalf of, primarily in terms of defense
to lift up and carry (away)
to take or bring someone along with
to cause or permit someone to move up onto an object, used especially in relation to boats, but with the possible associated meaning of welcoming or receiving

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to the lack of mercy or the refusal to be merciful
senses.comment: The meaning of ἀνέλεος and ἀνελεήμων is often expressed in highly idiomatic ways, for example, ‘to refuse to look at,’ ‘to turn one’s back on,’ or ‘to refuse to hear a person’s cries for help.’

senses.def: to assist in supplying what may be needed
senses.comment: As in the case of so many words with the meaning of ‘help,’ it may be necessary in some instances to use an equivalent phrase, for example, ‘to supply people with what they need’ or ‘to give to people what is necessary’ or ‘… what they should have.’

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: to give or commit oneself wholeheartedly to something
senses.comment: In a number of languages the concept of ‘devoting oneself to’ or ‘giving oneself wholly to’ is often expressed as ‘to do with one’s whole heart’ or ‘to want to do nothing else but.’|It is also possible to understand ἀντιλαμβάνομαι in 1 Timothy 6:2 in the sense of ‘to be benefited’ (see 65.48).

senses.def: to experience a benefit from someone
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀντιλαμβάνομαι in 1 Timothy 6:2, see 25.79.

senses.def: to declare that one will cause harm to someone, particularly if certain conditions are not met
senses.comment: Because of the implied reciprocity in ἀπειλέω and ἀπειλή, one may translate 1 Peter 2:23 as ‘when he suffered, he did not say he would make them suffer.’

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be known and thus secret, possibly in view of something being separate
senses.comment: The triple negation in Luke 8:17 may lead to some shift in a number of languages, for example, ‘everything which is secret now will be known.’

senses.def: to cause the process of burning to begin
senses.comment: As already noted in the series of terms listed in 14.63, languages differ appreciably in terms employed for different phases and results of burning. For example, to set something on fire for the sake of providing warmth may be expressed by quite a different term from that which is used in speaking of the process of setting something on fire in order to destroy it.

senses.def: to hold on to an object
to touch, with the implication of relatively firm contact
to cause some relatively light physical, moral, and/or spiritual harm to
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause something to be secure in the sense of something which could not be tampered with or opened
to fasten something securely
senses.comment: It is possible that in Acts 16:24 τὸ ξύλον designates ‘stocks,’ namely, two pieces of wood through which the feet could be placed so as to make a prisoner immobile (see 6.21).

senses.def: to cause people to rebel against or to reject authority
to move away from, with emphasis upon separation and possible lack of concern for what has been left
to abandon a former relationship or association, or to dissociate (a type of reversal of beginning to associate)
purposely to avoid association with someone
glosses: to have nothing to do with

senses.def: the action of ruling as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
senses.comment: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

senses.def: an area or district ruled by a king
senses.comment: Since in many areas of the world kingship is not known (that is to say, the succession of rulers within a family and by inheritance), it may not be possible to find a technical term meaning ‘kingdom.’ Usually, however, one may employ an expression which is roughly equivalent in meaning to ‘domain,’ so that, for example, the last part of Mark 6:23 may be rendered as ‘up to a half of the region which I rule.’

senses.def: a court official of Herod Agrippa I
a room in the Temple used as a treasury
senses.comment: It is possible that in John 8:20 γαζοφυλάκιον designates the offering boxes rather than the treasury itself (see γαζοφυλάκιον[b], 6.141). If one interprets γαζοφυλάκιον in John 8:20 as the offering boxes, then one may translate ‘he spoke these words near where the offering boxes were.’

senses.def: a large box in which offerings were placed
senses.comment: The offering box in the Temple was also referred to as δῶρον[b] (6.142).

senses.def: (derivative of γινώσκω[a] ‘to know,’ 28.1) one who knows, with the usual implication of to know well
to conduct oneself, with apparent focus upon overt daily behavior
to give detailed instructions as to what must be done
to arrange matters in a particular manner
a Christian who is criticized in 3 John 1:9
pertaining to that which is difficult to accomplish or do
a person appointed to rule over a particular area or constituency on behalf of a king
to pursue to the point of driving out
senses.comment: ἐκδιώκω in 1 Thessalonians 2:15 may also be understood in the sense of ‘to persecute’ (see 39.45).

senses.def: to systematically organize a program to oppress and harass people
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to persecute’ is simply ‘to cause to suffer,’ but persecution is also expressed in terms of ‘to be mean to’ or ‘to threaten’ or ‘to chase from place to place.’|For another interpretation of ἐκδιώκω in 1 Thessalonians 2:15, see 15.159.

senses.def: to shake something out or off, in order to get rid of an object or a substance
senses.comment: In a number of languages quite different terms for shaking will be required for the contexts of Acts 28:5 and Luke 9:5, since in the first instance it is an animate being which clings, and in the second instance it is simply a substance that adheres.|In a number of languages, however, the symbolic meaning of ‘shaking dust off one’s feet’ is not at all clear, so that it may be necessary to add a type of classifier to indicate that such an action symbolizes the breaking off of association. It is for this reason that the expression ἐκτιναξάμενος τὰ ἱμάτια in Acts 18:6 is often translated as ‘he protested by shaking the dust from his clothes.’

senses.def: a reflexive reference to the first person singular within the immediate context
senses.comment: For the plural, see 92.25.

senses.def: concealing oneself or proceeding secretly, while waiting for an appropriate opportunity to attack
senses.comment: Since ambushing is such a widespread method of warfare and private attack, there is usually little or no difficulty involved in finding an appropriate term and using it in what might be called an anticipatory sense, that is to say, the employment of an ambush despite the fact that it was not finally successful.

senses.def: to conform as a follower in a detailed or dependent manner
senses.comment: In some instances it may be necessary to translate ἐξακολουθήσαντες in 2 Peter 1:16 as ‘to use’ or ‘to repeat,’ since such expressions may fit the context more satisfactorily.

senses.def: to imitate behavior closely (in the NT the imitation involves wrong behavior)
senses.comment: An equivalent of this expression in 2 Peter 2:2 may be in some instances ‘many will live immoral lives just as they did.’

senses.def: to listen to, with the probable implication of one’s own interest
(derivative of ἐπιθυμέω[a] ‘to desire very much,’ 25.12) one who very much desires something, whether good or bad
to come together hurriedly to, toward, or at a particular location
glosses: to rush together to a place

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: any kind of clothing
(derivative of εὐνοῦχος[a] ‘eunuch,’ 9.25) to cause a person to be a eunuch
senses.comment: Sometimes one may render εὐνουχίζω as ‘to cause a person not to be able to have marital relations.’|In a number of languages the castration of a man is referred to by a term very different from what is employed in the case of the castration of an animal.

senses.def: (used with a reflexive pronoun) to live without engaging in sexual relations
a priest who was the father of John the Baptist
an OT prophet killed in the Temple
a son of Isaac and the elder twin brother of Jacob
a Jewish insurrectionist
one who causes someone to be healed
a son of Abraham and father of Jacob and Esau
to cause something to move down gradually
any fruit part of plants, including grain as well as pulpy fruit
senses.comment: A number of languages distinguish between different kinds of fruit. One common type of four-way distinction involves (1) nuts, (2) grain, (3) pulpy fruit surrounding a seed (the type of fruit primarily referred to in contexts containing καρπός[a]), and (4) fruit such as bananas, in which there is no noticeable seed. It is important in each instance to choose a term which will be applicable to the particular context.

senses.def: that which is harvested
(a figurative extension of meaning of καρπός[a] ‘fruit,’ 3.33) the natural result of what has been done
to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
(an idiom, literally: fruit gives) the ripening of fruit as a sign for the harvest to begin
(an idiom, literally: fruit of the womb) the child of a woman
(an idiom, literally: fruit of the genitals) descendant, as the result of the male role in procreation
to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
(an idiom, literally: to make fruit) to cause results to exist
to destroy completely by tearing down and dismantling
to destroy completely the efforts or work of someone else
senses.comment: In Romans 14:20 the work of God involves the building up of the community of faith.

senses.def: to cause to cease to exist
glosses: to cause to come to an end

senses.def: to completely invalidate something which has been in force
to experience the hospitality of someone, with principal focus upon lodging

senses.subdomain: In Front Of, Face To Face, In Back Of, Behind
senses.def: a position in front of an object, whether animate or inanimate, which is regarded as having a spacial orientation of front and back
(with the genitive) marking a participant whose viewpoint is relevant to an event
a brief statement of the main point of a previously given discourse
a sum of money
a Roman copper coin worth 1/4 of an assarion (Matthew 10:29) or 1/64 of a denarius (Luke 20:24)

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the bony framework of the head, especially the upper portion
glosses: skull (in the NT κρανίον is used only as a name for the hill of Golgotha)
senses.comment: In rendering κρανίου τόπος ‘place of the skull’ it may be necessary to indicate clearly the relationship between place and skull. A literal rendering of such a phrase might simply mean ‘a place where there was a skull.’ However the meaning of Golgotha has been interpreted generally as ‘a hill resembling a skull’ and therefore κρανίου τόπος may be more satisfactorily rendered as ‘a place resembling a skull’ or ‘a hill looking like a skull.’ See 93.453.

senses.def: to rule or reign over, with the implication in some contexts of lording it over
pertaining to being white or very light in color; applies to (parts of) the human body, animals, plants, inanimate objects
senses.comment: The term λευκός also occurs in John 4:35 in speaking of fields being ‘white for the harvest,’ but in a number of languages it would be quite impossible to use the same term for the ripe condition of a harvest as in the case of the color of wool or snow. Furthermore, there may be a serious difficulty in speaking of wool as being ‘white,’ since in many parts of the world, wool is not regarded as being particularly white.

senses.def: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source
a light made by burning a wick saturated with oil contained in a relatively small vessel
senses.comment: In some languages the closest equivalent of λαμπάς[b] and λύχνος is a kerosene lamp. What is to be avoided is a word which suggests a flashlight, which would of course be highly anachronistic.

senses.subdomain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking
senses.def: to bite with the teeth
senses.comment: In some languages it is important to distinguish clearly between three different kinds of biting: the biting of food, the biting of one’s own lips or tongue, and the biting of a person in a fight or quarrel.

senses.def: the valley of the Euphrates and Tigris rivers

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the uterus
senses.comment: For the total expression as an idiom, see 10.45. Rarely can one translate literally Luke 2:23 as ‘every male that opens the womb,’ since this is likely to refer to an adult male who first has sexual intercourse with a woman. The reference in Luke 2:23 is, of course, to the first male child which is born to a woman, and therefore an appropriate equivalent in many languages is ‘a woman’s first baby if it is a boy.’

senses.def: a construction of two flat stones between which grain was ground into flour by rotating the top stone
senses.comment: Some mills were relatively small and operated by hand and could well be considered as artifacts. Others, however, were quite large, and animals were used to rotate the upper stone.|In almost all parts of the world grain is ground in one way or another. Quite frequently mills are of the same general structure as those used in ancient times, in which two relatively large, round, flat stones were placed one on top of the other, and the grain was ground between the two stones. Grain entered the mill through a round hole in the upper stone, and the flour gradually emerged from around the edges of the two stones. In other parts of the world, however, grain is prepared by means of grinding stones called metates. In still other parts of the world, a mortar and pestle are used for the grinding or preparation of grain. In most contexts, what is important is either the large size of the stones or the function of grinding grain, not necessarily the particular form. However, in contexts which speak about tying a millstone to a man’s neck (see 7.69) and his being thrown into the depths of the sea, it is important to refer to relatively large stones which would cause a person to sink immediately. In such a context the use of a term for ‘mortar,’ especially one of wood, would hardly be appropriate since it would normally float. Frequently μύλος may be rendered as ‘stones for grinding grain.’ In other instances, even a more generic expression may be used, for example, ‘a large stone.’

senses.def: a large, round, flat stone, either upper or lower, used in grinding grain
senses.comment: μύλος[a] ‘mill’ (7.68) denotes a mill as a whole, while μύλος[b] denotes only one of the large flat stones of a mill. For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved in rendering μύλος[b] ‘millstone,’ see the discussion on μύλος[a] (7.68).

senses.def: the state of being very hungry, presumably for a considerable period of time and as the result of necessity rather than choice (compare νηστεία[a] ‘fasting,’ 53.65)
senses.comment: Terms referring to hunger often distinguish varying degrees of hunger and whether the hunger is by necessity or by choice.

senses.def: to shave the head or beard
a totality, with special emphasis upon the entity as a whole
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘your entire being.’ A substitute expression in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 may be ‘yourselves as one person.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to a tendency to become angry
a marker of coordinate negativized expressions (combination of the negative particle οὐ[a] 69.3, and the postpositive conjunction τέ[a] ‘and,’ 89.95)
a position near another location or object, usually with the implication of being alongside or close to
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects
(with the genitive) extension from a source which is actively involved in an activity or relation
(with the genitive) a marker of the agentive source of an activity, though often remote and indirect

senses.subdomain: Agent, Personal or Nonpersonal, Causative or Immediate, Direct or Indirect
senses.def: (with the genitive or dative) a marker of potential agent
(with the dative) marking a participant whose viewpoint is relevant to an event
a marker of that which is contrary to what should be or to expectation
a marker of contrast by means of an alternative
senses.comment: In a number of languages an alternative contrast must be expressed by a positive-negative sequence. For example, in Romans 1:25 one may translate ‘they worship and serve what God has created; they do not worship and serve the Creator himself.’

senses.def: a marker of association, with the implication of proximity to the so-called viewpoint character
a marker of cause or reason, with focus upon the source
a degree which is beyond that of a compared scale of extent
the state of being less than a given number or quantity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may seem strange as well as illogical to speak of ‘forty lashes minus one.’ Accordingly, one may translate ‘thirty-nine lashes’ in 2 Corinthians 11:24.

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: those beside him) the associates of a person, including family, neighbors, and friends
senses.comment: In some languages the idiom οἱ παρ’ αὐτοῦ is matched by other idiomatic expressions such as ‘those who share the same fire’ or ‘those who eat from the same pot.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to a relatively short period of time, with emphasis upon the temporary nature of the event or state
an apostle of Jesus Christ whose Hebrew name was Saul
Sergius Paulus, the governor of Cyprus
to illuminate an area surrounding an object
senses.comment: There may be difficulties involved in expressing the concept of ‘to shine around,’ since a more or less literal rendering might suggest a particular circle of light moving around an object. A more satisfactory way of dealing with this problem of ‘to shine around’ is to say ‘it was light there’ or ‘light shone upon me.’ In the case of Acts 26:13, one may translate ‘I saw a light from the sky there where I was.’

senses.def: a nutritionally rich, fatty quality
senses.comment: The text of Romans 11:17 is strange, for literally it reads ‘of the root of the richness.’ As may be easily understood, a number of scribal variations occur in different manuscripts.|Since the reference in Romans 11:17 is to the olive tree, the fruit of which produces so much oil, one can readily understand the basis for the extension of meaning. Some translations render πιότης simply as ‘sap’ (New English Bible), while others abandon completely the figure of speech, for example, TEV which has “you share the strong spiritual life.”|For another treatment of πιότης in Romans 11:17, see 65.7.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πιότης[a] ‘fatness,’ 3.59) a rich, valuable substance
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πιότης in Romans 11:17, see 3.59.

senses.def: (derivative of ποιέω[b] ‘to do,’ 42.7) one who does
one who produces literary texts, normally in poetic form

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the part of the leg below the ankle on which a person or animal stands and moves
senses.comment: In Revelation 10:1 (οἱ πόδες αὐτοῦ ὡς στῦλοι πυρός ‘his feet were like pillars of fire’) it is possible that πούς refers to the leg since the context of Revelation 10:1 would seem to favor this interpretation, but the meaning of ‘foot’ should not be excluded, especially since this passage refers to an image as part of a supernatural vision, and one cannot be certain of the specific intent.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to wash the feet, derived from the practice of washing the feet of any guest entering the home) to show sincere and gracious hospitality to someone
senses.comment: It is also possible that the idiom πόδας νίπτω means ‘to perform humble duties on behalf of someone’ (see 88.58).

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to wash the feet) to show humility by doing humble tasks
glosses: to behave in a humble manner
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πόδας νίπτω in 1 Timothy 5:10, see 34.59.

senses.def: (idioms, literally: to put at someone’s feet) to present something to someone who is reckoned as having superior status or position
(an idiom, literally: to make straight wheel tracks for the feet) to live or behave in strict conformance to a predetermined model for behavior
(idioms, literally under the feet of, and: footstool of the feet) to be under the complete control of someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is simply not possible to preserve the idiom ‘under the feet of,’ though in some instances one may use a parallel idiom, for example, ‘to stand on,’ so that 1 Corinthians 15:25 might be rendered ‘until he stands on all his enemies,’ but it is more likely that the idiom in this context is better rendered as ‘until he defeats all his enemies.’

senses.def: to exist in an evident manner
to exist subsequent to some temporal reference point

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: a wing of any flying creature
senses.comment: In Revelation 9:9, in which the apocalyptic locusts are mentioned, the expression ἡ φωνὴ τῶν πτερύγων may require a distinct term for ‘wings,’ since the wings of insects may be referred to by terms different from those employed in speaking of the wings of birds.

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: the movement of a liquid in some direction
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term referring to the flow of liquid may also be applied to the movement of any object, so that a literal rendering might be ‘the liquid moved.’ However, terms for ‘flow’ or ‘pour’ often differ substantially on the basis of the direction of the flow. For example, if the flow is relatively horizontal, and therefore slow, it may have one term, while if it is quite fast, another expression may be used, and if the flow is almost perpendicular (as in the case of pouring), a still different term is employed.

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a type of footwear consisting of a sole made of leather (or possibly wood) tied to the foot by means of thongs or straps
a rocky mountain on the peninsula of Sinai

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a small piece of cloth used as a towel, napkin, or face cloth
to cause someone to become stronger in the sense of more firm and unchanging in attitude or belief
to put or place something firmly in a location
(a Semitic idiom, literally: to fix one’s face) to make a decision, with emphasis upon finality
glosses: to make up one’s mind definitely
senses.comment: In order to express the meaning of ‘to decide firmly,’ it may be useful in some instances to translate ‘to decide and to refuse to change one’s mind’ or ‘to decide and not to change.’

senses.def: to express forceful differences of opinion without necessarily having a presumed goal of seeking a solution
to converse with someone, including a clear implication as to reciprocal response
to join with someone else in some severe effort
to give detailed instructions as to what must be done
to instruct someone to behave in a wise and becoming manner
fourteenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
pertaining to being uneven and rough, as of terrain
the state of being healthy, well (in contrast with sickness)
senses.comment: In a number of languages health is expressed only in terms of strength, for ‘to be well’ is ‘to be strong.’ In other languages, however, to be well or to be healthy is a negation of illness or sickness, so that in Mark 16:18 one may translate ‘they will place their hands on those who are sick and these people will become not sick.’

senses.def: pertaining to being accurate, as well as useful and beneficial
to put on and wear footwear (shoes, boots, or sandals)

senses.comment: φάραγξ, as ‘a narrow valley,’ differs from ‘a broad valley’ in the sense that one does not expect agriculture to be practiced at the bottom of a φάραγξ, while in the case of a broad valley, agriculture would be an assumed feature.

senses.def: a person greeted in Romans 16:14
a light-producing heavenly body, probably the morning star (a planet), but possibly the sun
senses.comment: The literal meaning of φωσφόρος is ‘that which bears light,’ but it is a conventional reference to the morning star, which in reality is not a star, but one of the brighter planets, usually Venus, but also Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, or even Saturn. In the one occurrence of this word in the NT, namely, 2 Peter 1:19, φωσφόρος is an indirect figurative reference to Jesus and his redemptive work, but it is extremely difficult in a number of languages to speak of ‘the light of the morning star shining in your hearts.’ One may sometimes say ‘… shines upon your hearts’ or possibly ‘… shines upon you and causes you to have new hearts’ or ‘… and illumines your minds.’

senses.def: to cause to eat so as to become satisfied
glosses: to cause to eat one’s fill
senses.comment: In some languages one may translate χορτάζω in Matthew 15:33 as ‘to cause to have as much as they wanted’ or ‘to give them food so that they didn’t want any more.’|In Matthew 5:6 (ὅτι αὐτοὶ χορτασθήσονται ‘because they will be satisfied’) the occurrence of χορτάζω should be interpreted as figurative, for it does not have specific reference to being satisfied with food (see 25.82).

senses.def: to eat, resulting in a state of being satisfied
senses.comment: One may render ‘were satisfied’ as ‘had all you wanted to eat’ or ‘did not want to eat any more.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of χορτάζομαι[a] ‘to eat one’s fill,’ 23.15) to be satisfied or content with some object or state
